summary: A group of Fairfield, Connecticut moms called the Mombies perform zombie dance routines on Halloween night to raise money for metastatic breast cancer research through the Cancer Couch Foundation. The group began in 2016 as a flash mob and has raised over $170,000 since 2017. The note covers how they plan in secret, the foundation's origin with the late Dr. Rebecca Timlin-Scalera, and why the founders emphasize fun.
one_line: Fairfield, Connecticut moms known as the Mombies dance as zombies each Halloween to raise money for metastatic breast cancer research via Cancer Couch.
key_facts: The Mombies perform an annual neighborhood zombie dance show on October 31 in the Fairfield Beach neighborhood of Fairfield, Connecticut.
Kate Garin, 39, an accountant in Fairfield, is a Mombie who spoke to Fox News Digital.
The Mombies include nurses, doctors, lawyers, accountants and more, and meet in secret for several weeks before Halloween.
Each year's music mashup always includes Michael Jackson's "Thriller," and the group works with professional choreographers.
The Mombies started in 2016 when Terry Davis, a Fairfield mom and human resources executive, organized a Halloween flash mob to surprise the neighborhood.
After the first year the group added "Dance to Donate" to raise money for the Cancer Couch.
Since 2017, the Mombies have raised over $170,000 for Cancer Couch.
Dr. Rebecca Timlin-Scalera created the Cancer Couch Foundation to accelerate research and treatment, and find a cure, for metastatic breast cancer; she died of the disease in 2019.
Tom Scalera says life expectancy for metastatic breast cancer patients is still just three to five years.
Cancer Couch is volunteer-run and privately funded, and 100% of money raised is matched and goes to research at labs at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Memorial Sloan Kettering.
The Scalera family covers all the foundation's expenses; their children Bella Scalera and Luca Scalera have been involved from the start.
Garin uses coffee grinds mixed with water to dirty costumes, and no Mombie does makeup alone.
Garin's daughter Victoria, 12, a competitive dancer, said she is proud of her mom for dancing and raising money for a cancer cure.
The group dances four or five times on Halloween night, and donations can be made at www.mombies.org.
